title: Oil as a source of conflict
subtitle: Black gold and power
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: A black liquid has brought down prime ministers, started wars and made empires rich. Here is why **oil** is never just energy.

hero.hook: For a century, whoever controls oil controls a share of world power.

blocks.text: **Oil** is not simply an energy source. It is the resource that has shaped world geopolitics most over the past century, and it still weighs on the balance of power today.

Its energy density and the ease of shipping it made it the engine of the industrial age, but also the trigger of crises and wars. Understanding oil means understanding why some countries grew so rich, and why others went to war over it.

sections.title: Black gold wakes up, from Pennsylvania to the Gulf

blocks.text: The age of industrial oil began in 1859, when the American engineer Edwin Drake drilled the first commercial well in Pennsylvania. But it was prospecting in the Middle East that really redrew the map of power: Iran in 1908, Iraq in 1927, then Saudi Arabia and Kuwait in 1938.
Before it became a fuel, Pennsylvania oil was sold in bottles as a miracle cure said to treat everything from rheumatism to baldness.

For decades, this wealth was exploited by a group of Western companies nicknamed the “Seven Sisters,” which imposed lopsided contracts and kept control of prices. Their grip built up a frustration that would later fuel demands for sovereignty.

sections.title: The birth of OPEC and the oil weapon

blocks.text: Against that dominance, five producing countries founded **OPEC** in Baghdad in 1960, to take back control of their resource and steady prices. But such wealth does not always bring the prosperity expected: this is the **[[Resource curse]]**, when an abundance of oil smothers every other sector and props up authoritarian regimes.

The breaking point came with the oil shock of 1973. In the middle of the **[[Yom Kippur War]]**, the Arab members of OPEC declared an embargo against Israel's allies. Within six months, the price of a barrel had quadrupled.

blocks.caption: The 1973 oil shock brought long lines at gas stations across the Western world

blocks.text: Western economies, built on a steady flow of cheap crude, fell into a crisis that combined high inflation with stalled growth, forcing states to rethink their energy security.

Oil became central to most of the big conflicts of the late 20th century. One of the earliest examples was the attempt by the Iranian prime minister **[[Mohammad Mossadegh]]** to nationalize the British oil companies in 1951, before he was overthrown in 1953 by a Western-backed coup.

The Persian Gulf became the epicenter of chronic instability. In 1990, Iraq's invasion of Kuwait threatened the world market directly. The Gulf War of 1991 was as much about stopping Iraq from controlling a huge share of global reserves as about freeing a sovereign state.
During the Gulf War in 1991, the oil well fires lit by the Iraqi army were so vast that they could be seen from space, and they pushed local temperatures down by several degrees.

The same script played out with the Iraq War of 2003. Today the pattern has moved into civil wars: in Venezuela, Nigeria and Libya, control of the wells and the refineries is still the sinew of internal struggle, because whoever owns the oil can pay for an army.

Around 2010, the geopolitics of oil went through a genuine technical earthquake. Thanks to hydraulic fracturing, the United States began producing **[[shale oil]]** on a massive scale. That shift made it the world's leading producer and cut its historic dependence on the Middle East.

For a while, this new abundance quieted fears about peak oil, the theory that predicts an inevitable end to the resource. Supply did become more varied, but the tensions did not disappear: they moved onto the transport routes, such as the Strait of Hormuz, and onto contested new fields in the eastern Mediterranean.

The 1973 oil shock, which quadrupled the price of a barrel after the Arab embargo, turned oil into a major geopolitical weapon and exposed how vulnerable developed countries are to their own energy dependence.
